title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: In chemical manufacturing, the income statement promises margins, but the working capital cycle collects the rent.
epigraph.author: Institutional Forensic Desk

web_blocks.html: Laurus Labs sells through three distinct channels, each with its own pricing, lead times, and cash cycles [5, 13, 18]:

1. Global Institutional Tenders (PEPFAR, Global Fund, LMIC Ministries): ARV tablets and bulk APIs go into pooled donor tenders [13]. Sites need WHO prequalification and USFDA tentative approval [13]. Annual tender awards and donor budgets drive volumes, which exposes sales to periodic destocking and price cuts [13, 16].
2. Innovator CDMO Master Service Agreements (MSAs): Human, animal, and crop-science CDMO contracts take 3 to 5 years to qualify, moving from lab routes to commercial supply [5, 15, 17]. Once a plant is named in an innovator's drug filing, switching costs are high [15]. Even so, quarterly shipments stay lumpy around client trial timelines [15].
3. Regulated Generic Formulations & APIs (US, EU, Canada): Non-ARV tablets rely on USFDA ANDA approvals (39 approved out of 51+ filings, with ~12 pending) and Western distributor deals [18].

web_blocks.title: Working Capital & Capex Reinvestment Friction
paragraphs: FY26 CFO rose to ₹1,624 Cr, yet working capital remains heavy [1]. Inventory Days climbed to 317 days, up from 285 in FY25 and 222 in FY23 [1]. Debtor Days stood at 115 days, keeping the Cash Conversion Cycle at 263 days [1]. Meanwhile, CWIP jumped to ₹1,282 Cr by Sep 2026, with ₹3,000+ Cr of multi-year capex planned [1].

book_paragraphs: Follow a single rupee through Laurus Labs in FY26 and you immediately see both the brilliance of the operating model and its chief constraint. Out of every ₹100 of sales, ₹73.80 covered raw materials, scientists, power, and plant overhead, leaving ₹26.20 in operating profit. Subtract ₹7.05 for depreciation, ₹2.51 for interest, and ₹4.29 for taxes (plus ₹0.69 of other income), and ₹13.06 dropped to the bottom line.

Because depreciation is a non-cash charge and working capital stabilized in FY26, Cash Flow from Operations actually reached ₹23.84 per ₹100 of revenue—₹1,624 crore in total. That is genuine cash generation. But look at the very next line: ₹15.62 out of every ₹100 went straight back out the door into reactors, peptide synthesizers, and fermentation tanks, leaving ₹8.22 of Free Cash Flow.

Why is the business so hungry for both working capital and fixed capital? Part of the answer is chemistry—multi-step synthesis and long CDMO qualification cycles require carrying raw materials and work-in-progress across 317 inventory days. The other part is ambition: building 7,200+ kiloliters of reactors, 16,000 liters of peptide capacity, and 180 kiloliters of fermentation tanks takes heavy upfront steel before commercial batches ever hit full utilization.

Now let us follow a single ₹100 note as it enters Laurus Labs' door in FY26 and trace what is left by the time it reaches free cash flow. You and I can learn more from that ₹100 waterfall than from twenty pages of management slides.

Out of every ₹100 of FY26 revenue (₹6,813 Cr total), raw materials and intermediates consume roughly ₹41.20—meaning Laurus keeps ₹58.80 in gross margin, a reflection of rising CDMO mix and backward integration. Employee costs take ₹12.40 (funding over 6,500 employees including 1,050+ R&D scientists), and other manufacturing, power, and compliance expenses consume another ₹22.10. That leaves ₹24.30 in operating EBITDA—already a healthy recovery from the FY24 trough.

But watch what happens below the EBITDA line. Depreciation consumes ₹6.50 out of every ₹100 because Laurus has built over ₹5,000 Cr of gross fixed assets across 11+ regulatory-approved sites. Finance costs take another ₹2.80 to service ₹2,625 Cr of gross borrowings. After ₹0.60 of other income and ₹4.20 in taxes, net profit (PAT) settles around ₹13.90 per ₹100 of sales (₹890 Cr total PAT).

Here is where forensic accounting separates the amateur from the institutional analyst: in FY26, Laurus generated ₹25.40 of Cash Flow from Operations (CFO) per ₹100 of revenue (₹1,624 Cr)—182% of reported PAT—thanks to disciplined working-capital release after the prior buildout. Yet capital expenditure consumed ₹16.65 per ₹100 of revenue (₹1,064 Cr), leaving ₹8.75 per ₹100 (₹560 Cr) in true Free Cash Flow.

That waterfall teaches a vital lesson about Laurus Labs' unit economics: the P&L looks asset-light when utilization is high, but the cash-flow statement reminds you that every rupee of incremental CDMO revenue demands heavy upfront steel, glass-lined reactors, and 317 days of inventory sitting across raw materials, work-in-progress, and validated commercial campaigns.

Understanding how a product is sold and delivered is where good business analysis turns into great cash-flow forecasting. In Laurus Labs' ARV and Generic FDF businesses, distribution runs through institutional tenders (WHO, Global Fund, PEPFAR) and regulated-market generic wholesalers in the US and Europe. Working capital here is driven by tender shipment schedules and regulatory batch-release testing.

In the Innovator CDMO business, there are no distributors or retail dealers at all. The go-to-market engine is a direct scientific relationship between Laurus's business-development chemists and the CMC (Chemistry, Manufacturing, and Controls) heads of global pharma, animal-health, and agrochemical companies. Qualification takes three to five years, which creates formidable switching costs—but it also means Laurus must build dedicated capacity *before* commercial revenues arrive, locking cash into Capital Work-in-Progress and 317 days of inventory.

When we traced ₹100 of FY26 revenue down to free cash flow, we saw both sides of that coin: ₹58.80 of gross margin and ₹25.40 of operating cash flow per ₹100 of sales proved the underlying profitability of the new mix, while ₹16.65 of capex per ₹100 reminded us that Laurus must constantly reinvest steel and reactors to keep the flywheel turning.

To appreciate why working capital is so critical to Laurus Labs' unit economics, follow a single commercial CDMO batch from raw material to cash collection. Because innovator clients demand uninterrupted supply security for patented drugs, Laurus must procure specialized regulatory starting materials months in advance, hold work-in-progress across six to ten synthetic steps, complete analytical release testing, and ship globally—creating a 317-day inventory footprint in FY26.
When commercial volumes surge, as they did in H1 FY27, fixed-cost absorption lifts EBITDA margins above 33% and releases cash. When orders pause, that same working-capital pipe absorbs cash rapidly.

If there is one operational metric you should track alongside gross margin in Chapter 3, it is cash conversion cycle discipline. Bringing 317 inventory days down even by 40 to 50 days as commercial CDMO shipments normalize would unlock hundreds of crores of cash internally—reducing reliance on external borrowings during the ₹3,000+ Cr capex build.

Every rupee of gross margin earned inside Laurus Labs' reactors still has to navigate the physical realities of pharmaceutical logistics: multi-month regulatory raw-material lead times, work-in-progress buffers across complex multi-step syntheses, and finished-goods release testing. That physical pipeline is why FY26 inventory stood at 317 days and why capex consumed ₹16.65 out of every ₹100 of revenue. Watching how fast that working-capital and capex intensity moderates as commercial CDMO campaigns mature will tell you far more than any headline EPS beat.

book_callouts.title: The 3-to-5 Year Qualification Gate
paragraphs: In innovator CDMO, you cannot buy market share with discounts. Every molecule requires 3–5 years of process development, stability batches, and regulatory filing before commercial annuity begins—which explains both the sticky moat once won and the long capex payback lag.
